stories.headline: Tamil Nadu on rain alert? Bay of Bengal system may intensify into Cyclone Arnab by October 26
stories.title: Tamil Nadu on rain alert? Bay of Bengal system may intensify into Cyclone Arnab by October 26
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: A new low-pressure area over the southeast Bay of Bengal could intensify into Cyclone Arnab by October 26, raising concerns over heavier rainfall in Tamil Nadu amid the active northeast monsoon.

Chennai: With the northeast monsoon already bringing heavy rain to Tamil Nadu, a fresh weather system over the southeast Bay of Bengal could worsen the state's rainfall woes and intensify into Cyclone Arnab by October 26.
A weather department update reported by Dinamalar identified a new low-pressure area over the southeast Bay of Bengal.
The system is expected to strengthen into a depression the following day, before potentially developing into a cyclone on October 26.
If it develops into a cyclone, the system is expected to be named Arnab.
Bangladesh proposed the name under the regional cyclone-naming system.
The emerging system comes as Tamil Nadu is already witnessing heavy rain amid an increasingly active northeast monsoon.
Its further development could intensify rainfall across several districts, raising concerns about additional pressure on the state's civic infrastructure.
Heavier downpours can strain urban drainage systems, disrupt road movement and complicate routine civic operations, particularly in areas already experiencing persistent monsoon rain.
However, the available weather update does not specify which districts could receive the heaviest rainfall or provide estimates of expected precipitation.
There is also no confirmed information in the update on the system's projected landfall location, anticipated wind speeds or likely trajectory.
The precise extent of its impact on Tamil Nadu therefore remains uncertain.

stories.headline: IMD Update: Possible Bay of Bengal Cyclone by Monday; AP, Odisha on Alert
stories.title: IMD Update: Possible Bay of Bengal Cyclone by Monday; AP, Odisha on Alert
stories.summary: A parent low-pressure area is expected to move west-north-westwards over Bay, intensifying into a deep depression by Sunday and a cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay by Monday morning
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Bay of Bengal is brewing a potentially powerful cyclone, with the India Meteorological Department (IMD) hinting at its formation by Monday as a parent low-pressure area emerged over the south-east and adjoining east-central Bay on Friday morning.
The system is expected to move west-north-westwards, intensify into a deep depression by Sunday, and become a cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay by Monday morning.
It is then forecast to strengthen further and head towards the north Andhra Pradesh and adjoining south Odisha coasts over the next two days.
Global models suggest it could reach at least severe cyclonic storm intensity.
Meanwhile, another low-pressure area is holding sway over the south-east Arabian Sea, off the south Kerala coast, setting the stage for an intriguing interaction between the two systems.
The European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts had suggested last week that the Arabian Sea low and the developing Bay cyclone could feed off each other, helping both systems strengthen.
Under that scenario, the Bay system would approach the Andhra Pradesh-Odisha coast, while its Arabian Sea counterpart would move northwards along the Kerala-Karnataka coast towards Goa.
The IMD, however, envisages a different twist to the tale.

Strong south-westerly flows feeding the systems could steer the Arabian Sea low back across the South Peninsula towards the south-west Bay, close to south Tamil Nadu and north Sri Lanka, from where it originated.
Thereafter, it could merge with the developing cyclone over the larger Bay.
Such a convergence could give the north-east monsoon another powerful burst next week, keeping the Southern Peninsula firmly in the rain belt even as the Bay system gathers strength.
Another rain-bearing system is in the forecast as Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal recover impressively from a distressing south-west monsoon season between June and September.

stories.headline: Architect of ambition: What 25 years of Modi means for business
stories.title: Architect of ambition: What 25 years of Modi means for business
stories.summary: When I founded ReNew in 2011, the hardest conversations I had weren’t with engineers, policymakers or bankers. They were with investors.The question was always a version of: Will the India of today still be there 20 years from now?Renewable energy is a business of long horizons. A project built today must generate reliable returns for 25 years. Investors were not evaluating a power plant; they were evaluating a country. They wanted to know whether policies would endure, infrastructure would materialise, institutions would strengthen, and whether India could maintain direction over decades rather than months.What they were looking for was constancy. Predictability.I have met many political leaders who follow where markets lead. It is rare to meet one who decides where a country should go and then patiently builds the road.Looking back over Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s 25 years in public life, first as Gujarat chief minister and then as prime minister, that quality stands out the most. Not simply ambition, but constancy of ambition. An ability to see something before it becomes obvious, pursue it patiently, and remain committed until a nation begins to believe in it too.Also Read: How India has learnt to build the impossiblePursuit of executionI have had the opportunity to meet Prime Minister Modi on several occasions. That instinct, to see beyond the next election, pursue relentlessly and govern for the next generation, is perhaps the most valuable thing a leader can offer an entrepreneur like me. Businesses can adapt to almost any direction. What we struggle with is uncertainty.That sense of certainty and pursuit of execution that Prime Minister Modi has brought has changed the feel of India. As I travel across the country to our project sites, I find it in thousands of everyday scenes. Village after village remains lit long after sunset. Roads reach places that once felt disconnected from opportunity. Border settlements that seemed remote are now linked by highways, telecommunications and reliable power.Towns like Sanand, Dholera, Hosur, Thrissur and Sri City, which barely registered on the economic map 25 years ago, are today attracting global capital, producing for international markets and creating opportunities for millions. Small towns that we once simply drove through are now crowded with warehouses, apartment blocks, hospitals, hotels, logistics parks and bustling marketplaces.Women who once organised daily life around the absence of toilets, reliable electricity or clean cooking fuel increasingly enjoy a degree of dignity and convenience. Small businesses accept digital payments from customers. Young creators from places far from India’s traditional centres of opportunity now participate in a national economy connected by roads, phones and digital networks.The biggest change is not any individual programme. It is that prosperity feels more widely distributed.One senses movement. One senses confidence. Above all, one senses that millions more Indians now expect their children to live better lives than they did. Of course, none of this emerged from a vacuum.Connective tissueIndia’s progress did not begin in 2014. It was built upon institutions, reforms and capabilities accumulated over decades. But the defining feature of Prime Minister Modi’s era has been the game-changing acceleration, scale and execution brought to those foundations.In earlier years, the transformation often happened incrementally and slowly. A road here. A bank account there. A digital platform. A tax reform. An electricity connection. A logistics corridor. Individually, each reform seemed limited.Under Prime Minister Modi’s leadership, they were pursued together. Only because someone at the top insisted they be pursued together did they form the connective tissue that allowed the economy to function with greater coherence. They created conditions for private capital to be deployed, not merely promised.They were accompanied by stronger public institutions and public sector enterprises, not as relics of an earlier era but as instruments of national capability. Whether securing oil supplies, acquiring critical minerals, supporting defence manufacturing, kickstarting clean energy markets or helping create new industrial ecosystems, they increasingly acted with the confidence of a country determined not merely to participate in global supply chains, but to shape them.Brick by brick, India has been building. Faster in some areas, slower in the others, but with a visible spine connecting the effort. That confidence has also been tested.Over the last decade, India has navigated a pandemic, global supply chain disruptions, energy price shocks, conflicts in Ukraine and West Asia, and a more fragmented geopolitical landscape. Through these tests, one sensed a country increasingly confident in its capacity to act, whether by vaccinating hundreds of millions of people, evacuating citizens from conflict zones, or maintaining stability and growth amid global turbulence.The consistency sends a powerful signal beyond India’s shores. It tells a lender in Singapore or a pension fund in Toronto that the direction will not reverse with political cycles or global uncertainty. Capital, which is risk-averse, grows braver in the presence of that kind of leadership.Yet, in my view, the most consequential change may have occurred in a field that will define the coming century: Energy and climate.Also Read: When households became shareholders: The quiet story of India's balance sheetDeeper transformationFor much of modern history, energy security was synonymous with access to oil and gas. Economic growth depended on resources concentrated in distant geographies, often vulnerable to conflict and disruption. Prime Minister Modi recognised earlier than most that the clean energy transition could offer India a different path.I remember in 2015 when he announced India’s bold renewable energy ambitions to the world. I was in Glasgow in 2021 when he announced India’s commitment to net zero by 2070. Many international observers did not expect India to make such a pledge. But the significance of those moments went far beyond the targets themselves. They signalled a deeper transformation.Clean energy is now meeting most of the growth in India’s electricity demand, helping power factories, irrigation pumps, Global Capability Centres and the digital economy. India is manufacturing equipment, building transmission networks, investing in storage and developing cleaner fuels. We are on the path to insulating ourselves from being held hostage to crises or decisions made elsewhere.In fact, the availability of abundant clean energy is helping position India as one of the world’s most attractive destinations for data centres, advanced manufacturing and semiconductors—new-age industries creating opportunities for further prosperity.Underlying all of this is a simple but profound idea: Clean energy is not merely climate policy. It is economic security. It is strategic autonomy. It is nation building.ReNew is, in many ways, a product of Prime Minister Modi’s larger vision.Over fifteen years, we have grown into one of India’s largest clean energy companies, with a balance sheet of more than $11 billion and a pipeline approaching 28 GW. We generate almost a tenth of India’s solar and wind power, have created over 100,000 jobs directly and indirectly, and have connected global capital to the Indian opportunity.But ours is only one of many such stories. Across sectors, entrepreneurs have built companies, industries and capabilities because a leader set the ambition, built the ground beneath it and stayed the course. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi (front R) and French President Emmanuel Macron (front L) pose with world leaders and representatives for a group picture at the start of the founding conference of the International Solar Alliance in New Delhi on March 11, 2018. The International Solar Alliance (ISA) organizes more than 121 "sunshine" countries that are situated or have territory between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn, with the aim of boosting solar energy output in an effort to reduce global dependence on fossil fuels. (Photo by Ludovic MARIN / AFP)A very different futureCan we provide round-the-clock clean, reliable power to every home, factory and data centre? Can we secure critical minerals, deepen manufacturing capabilities, master artificial intelligence and create globally competitive industries in technologies that are only now emerging? Can we ensure that every Indian enjoys cleaner air, better opportunities and a quality of life that matches the best in the world?These questions will require patient institution building, long-term investment and relentless execution. They will demand the same discipline that got us here.India has been fortunate to have, in Prime Minister Modi, an architect and a visionary who understands these issues intuitively and is willing to spearhead them. Under his leadership, India has begun to believe in its own capacity to build at the scale of its ambitions.Once a nation acquires that belief, its future begins to look very different from its past. This self confidence, and its manifestation in action, will be Prime Minister Modi’s most enduring contribution to India.

Renewable energy is a business of long horizons.
A project built today must generate reliable returns for 25 years.
Investors were not evaluating a power plant; they were evaluating a country.
They wanted to know whether policies would endure, infrastructure would materialise, institutions would strengthen, and whether India could maintain direction over decades rather than months.
What they were looking for was constancy.
Predictability.
I have met many political leaders who follow where markets lead.
It is rare to meet one who decides where a country should go and then patiently builds the road.
Looking back over Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s 25 years in public life, first as Gujarat chief minister and then as prime minister, that quality stands out the most.
Not simply ambition, but constancy of ambition.
An ability to see something before it becomes obvious, pursue it patiently, and remain committed until a nation begins to believe in it too.
Pursuit of execution.
I have had the opportunity to meet Prime Minister Modi on several occasions.
That instinct, to see beyond the next election, pursue relentlessly and govern for the next generation, is perhaps the most valuable thing a leader can offer an entrepreneur like me.
Businesses can adapt to almost any direction.
What we struggle with is uncertainty.
That sense of certainty and pursuit of execution that Prime Minister Modi has brought has changed the feel of India.
As I travel across the country to our project sites, I find it in thousands of everyday scenes.
Village after village remains lit long after sunset.
Roads reach places that once felt disconnected from opportunity.
Border settlements that seemed remote are now linked by highways, telecommunications and reliable power.

Towns like Sanand, Dholera, Hosur, Thrissur and Sri City, which barely registered on the economic map 25 years ago, are today attracting global capital, producing for international markets and creating opportunities for millions.
Small towns that we once simply drove through are now crowded with warehouses, apartment blocks, hospitals, hotels, logistics parks and bustling marketplaces.
Women who once organised daily life around the absence of toilets, reliable electricity or clean cooking fuel increasingly enjoy a degree of dignity and convenience.
Small businesses accept digital payments from customers.
Young creators from places far from India’s traditional centres of opportunity now participate in a national economy connected by roads, phones and digital networks.
The biggest change is not any individual programme.
It is that prosperity feels more widely distributed.
One senses movement.
One senses confidence.
Above all, one senses that millions more Indians now expect their children to live better lives than they did.
Of course, none of this emerged from a vacuum.
Connective tissue.
India’s progress did not begin in 2014.
It was built upon institutions, reforms and capabilities accumulated over decades.
But the defining feature of Prime Minister Modi’s era has been the game-changing acceleration, scale and execution brought to those foundations.
In earlier years, the transformation often happened incrementally and slowly.
A road here.
A bank account there.
A digital platform.
A tax reform.
An electricity connection.
A logistics corridor.
Individually, each reform seemed limited.
Under Prime Minister Modi’s leadership, they were pursued together.
Only because someone at the top insisted they be pursued together did they form the connective tissue that allowed the economy to function with greater coherence.
They created conditions for private capital to be deployed, not merely promised.
They were accompanied by stronger public institutions and public sector enterprises, not as relics of an earlier era but as instruments of national capability.

Whether securing oil supplies, acquiring critical minerals, supporting defence manufacturing, kickstarting clean energy markets or helping create new industrial ecosystems, they increasingly acted with the confidence of a country determined not merely to participate in global supply chains, but to shape them.
Brick by brick, India has been building.
Faster in some areas, slower in the others, but with a visible spine connecting the effort.
That confidence has also been tested.
Over the last decade, India has navigated a pandemic, global supply chain disruptions, energy price shocks, conflicts in Ukraine and West Asia, and a more fragmented geopolitical landscape.

Through these tests, one sensed a country increasingly confident in its capacity to act, whether by vaccinating hundreds of millions of people, evacuating citizens from conflict zones, or maintaining stability and growth amid global turbulence.
The consistency sends a powerful signal beyond India’s shores.
It tells a lender in Singapore or a pension fund in Toronto that the direction will not reverse with political cycles or global uncertainty.
Capital, which is risk-averse, grows braver in the presence of that kind of leadership.
Yet, in my view, the most consequential change may have occurred in a field that will define the coming century: Energy and climate.
Deeper transformationFor much of modern history, energy security was synonymous with access to oil and gas.
Economic growth depended on resources concentrated in distant geographies, often vulnerable to conflict and disruption.
Prime Minister Modi recognised earlier than most that the clean energy transition could offer India a different path.
I remember in 2015 when he announced India’s bold renewable energy ambitions to the world.
I was in Glasgow in 2021 when he announced India’s commitment to net zero by 2070.
Many international observers did not expect India to make such a pledge.
But the significance of those moments went far beyond the targets themselves.
They signalled a deeper transformation.
Clean energy is now meeting most of the growth in India’s electricity demand, helping power factories, irrigation pumps, Global Capability Centres and the digital economy.
India is manufacturing equipment, building transmission networks, investing in storage and developing cleaner fuels.
We are on the path to insulating ourselves from being held hostage to crises or decisions made elsewhere.

In fact, the availability of abundant clean energy is helping position India as one of the world’s most attractive destinations for data centres, advanced manufacturing and semiconductors—new-age industries creating opportunities for further prosperity.
Underlying all of this is a simple but profound idea: Clean energy is not merely climate policy.
It is economic security.
It is strategic autonomy.
It is nation building.
ReNew is, in many ways, a product of Prime Minister Modi’s larger vision.
Over fifteen years, we have grown into one of India’s largest clean energy companies, with a balance sheet of more than $11 billion and a pipeline approaching 28 GW.
We generate almost a tenth of India’s solar and wind power, have created over 100,000 jobs directly and indirectly, and have connected global capital to the Indian opportunity.
But ours is only one of many such stories.
Across sectors, entrepreneurs have built companies, industries and capabilities because a leader set the ambition, built the ground beneath it and stayed the course.

(Photo by Ludovic MARIN / AFP)A very different futureCan we provide round-the-clock clean, reliable power to every home, factory and data centre?
Can we secure critical minerals, deepen manufacturing capabilities, master artificial intelligence and create globally competitive industries in technologies that are only now emerging?
Can we ensure that every Indian enjoys cleaner air, better opportunities and a quality of life that matches the best in the world?
These questions will require patient institution building, long-term investment and relentless execution.
They will demand the same discipline that got us here.
India has been fortunate to have, in Prime Minister Modi, an architect and a visionary who understands these issues intuitively and is willing to spearhead them.
Under his leadership, India has begun to believe in its own capacity to build at the scale of its ambitions.
Once a nation acquires that belief, its future begins to look very different from its past.
This self confidence, and its manifestation in action, will be Prime Minister Modi’s most enduring contribution to India.

article_sentences: The Keralam government on Friday ordered an anti-corruption investigation against former Kannur district panchayat president and Communist Party of India (Marxist) [CPI(M)] leader P.P. Divya.

Officials said Home Minister Ramesh Chennithala sanctioned the inquiry into the award of a ₹12-crore contract to a private firm to construct modular toilets, allegedly without inviting open tenders and thereby bypassing competitive bidding.
By sanctioning the probe, under Section 17 (A) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, Mr Chennithala opened the door to the Vigilance investigation.
According to Vigilance and Anti-Corruption Bureau (VACB) officials, government sanction does not preclude a preliminary inquiry or require the outright registration of an FIR.

They noted that, in earlier cases, the VACB had conducted a preliminary inquiry to determine whether the allegations disclosed a cognisable offence under the Prevention of Corruption (PC) Act before registering an FIR.
They said the Supreme Court, in several orders, had reiterated the need for a preliminary inquiry before registering a Vigilance offence against those who held public office.
However, officials said registering an FIR by the VACB would automatically trigger an Enforcement Directorate (ED) investigation under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA).

Earlier, the Kerala Students Union (KSU) vice president had moved the government, alleging that Ms Divya and her husband, V.P. Ajith, had links with the firm and the company was a front for the CPI(M) leader.
Both Ms Divya and Mr Ajith denied the accusation and said the complaint was politically motivated.

The CPI(M) had removed Ms Divya from the post of Kannur district president after the police booked her on the charge of abetting the death by suicide of former Kannur Additional District Magistrate Naveen Babu.

Naveen Babu’s death, following an allegedly defamatory speech by Ms Divya at his farewell function at the Kannur District Collectorate, put the CPI(M) on the defensive in Kannur and his home district of Pathanamthitta.

The Communist Party of India (CPI), which held the Revenue portfolio in the previous Left Democratic Front (LDF) dispensation, demanded Ms Divya’s prosecution and cautioned the CPI(M) against giving her any political protection.
